### What is Marigold?
URL: https://earthdaily.github.io/documentation/mining/using-marigold/what-is-marigold/

# What is Marigold?

## Marigold is a GIS user interface built on top of the EarthDaily platform and tailored to exploration geologists.

Marigold revolutionizes mineral exploration workflows by simplifying the process of accessing and analyzing remote sensing data.

### Working with Marigold

#### Fast

EarthDaily and Marigold significantly decreases the time needed to prepare for mineral exploration by up to 85%. Analyzing data and collaborating on projects with colleagues becomes simpler and more efficient.

#### Streamlined

All the tools you need are in a single, easy-to-use interface — no more switching between applications or working with complex code.

#### Global

Our Bare Earth Composite gives users access to the clearest pixel everywhere on Earth. Work with analysis-ready data to derive insights from the smallest to the largest scale.

### Getting started with Marigold

#### New to remote sensing?

Learn how remotely sensed data provides valuable insights we can't capture on the ground.

#### Looking to jump in?

Hit the ground running by accessing Marigold, adding new layers and mineral targets, and running a spectral similarity algorithm to identify potentially prospective areas.

#### Ready to keep learning?

Follow along in some of our case studies to learn how to spot different types of mineralization from start to finish.

---

### Introducing Marigold v2
URL: https://earthdaily.github.io/documentation/mining/using-marigold/introducing-marigold-v2/

# Introducing Marigold

## Announcing the release of Marigold v2.0

Access the new URL for Marigold v2.0 at . Be sure to update your bookmarks to smoothly transition to the latest version. Upon your first login you will notice the following:

- **Token-Free Login:** Users are no longer required to enter a token upon their first login.
- **One-Time Migration of Save Files and Bookmarks:** When logging into the new Marigold for the first time, users will see a progress indicator for the one-time migration of their save files and bookmarks.

---

### What's New

**Intuitive Layer Masking**

Marigold v2.0 introduces layer masking using vector masks in addition to raster masks. This reduces false positives and supports multi-feature vectors.

**Live Layer Adjustments**

Preview adjustments before finalizing layer updates, allowing for more confident and precise refinement.

**Vector Catalog**

A new vector catalog — initially including a dataset of global faults — enables users to analyze and work with vector data.

---

### What's Improved

**Improved Histograms and Spectral Plots**

Users can now zoom in on specific ranges of histograms for more detailed adjustment of min/max values.

**Improved Band Checkboxes**

Improved scheme for band checkboxes related to transforms, classifications, and the raster calculator tool.

**Enhanced Data Export**

Exported file names now reflect the name of the band for easier identification and organization.

**On-the-Fly Canny Edge Detection**

Results from the Canny edge detection tool are now generated on the fly within seconds, replacing the previous Tasks service.

**Paginated Saved Projects**

Saved projects are now paginated in the "Load project" dialog, with search functionality.

**Enhanced Band Drop Downs**

Band drop downs in the layer adjustment interface now fill the dialog's width, making long band names more readable.

**Version Indicator**

Moved to the bottom right of the interface for an unobstructed view of the layer list.

---

### What's Fixed

**Spectral Data Query Locations**

The application now correctly retains the position of spectral queries in `.sav` files.

**Increased Saved Project View Limit**

The number of saved projects viewable in a single page has been increased to 50.

---

For more information see the [Marigold documentation](https://docs.descarteslabs.com/packaged-analytics/ame/using-marigold.html).

### Recovering Work with Autosave
URL: https://earthdaily.github.io/documentation/mining/using-marigold/avoiding-lost-work-in-marigold/

# Recovering work in Marigold with the Autosave feature

## Gone in the blink of an eye? Chances are your hard work can be saved.

Periodically saving your Marigold workspace is the best way to ensure that your layers and products stay just the way you want them. Occasionally though, your session may close without saving. In many cases you can recover your work using Marigold's autosave feature.

### Marigold has closed without saving

This primarily happens due to timing-out. Marigold sessions are programmed to time-out after an hour of inactivity. You may return to your computer to see a notification that your connection to the server has been lost.

Don't panic! Simply click **Refresh** and Marigold will reload into a new session. To recover your work:

1. Click **Load** from the top panel menu
2. Select `autosave.sav` and click **Load Project**
3. Click **Save** from the top panel menu and name your saved file

### Tips and Considerations

- The autosave feature only works on one Marigold session at a time. While Marigold supports a user working in separate instances simultaneously, the `autosave.sav` file will only be associated with one.
- The `autosave.sav` file backs up your work every five minutes, so some work may be lost if Marigold closed due to a rare crash or accidental closure.
- To avoid accidentally closing Marigold with other browser tabs, consider installing Marigold as an "App" to keep it in its own window with a taskbar/desktop shortcut.
- Occasionally create versioned workspaces by clicking **Save** and appending a version number to the file name.

---

### Compositional Mapping Tool
URL: https://earthdaily.github.io/documentation/mining/using-marigold/compositional-mapping-tool-reko-diq/

# Hyperspectral Compositional Mapping Tool

## A step-by-step walkthrough using the Reko Diq porphyry system as a case study.

### Introduction

This tool was developed to help make characterization and quantification of hyperspectral mapping easier and more consistent for geologists who are not remote sensing experts. It includes assessment of mineral group relative abundance and compositional differentiation for selected mineral groups. The tool helps geologists build on multispectral compositional mapping results and derive quality analyses from hyperspectral data.

> **Note:** This tool does **not** work with multispectral (MS) data such as Sentinel-2, ASTER, or the Fused BEC.

The tool can be found under the **Hyperspectral** drop-down menu in the Marigold Mineral Processing Toolbox.

---

### Step 1 — Verify the Input Hyperspectral (HSI) Dataset

EnMap, PRISMA, EMIT, or other airborne/spaceborne hyperspectral datasets all work with the tool. The dataset should be cleaned using the **Data Statistical Analysis Tool** to remove bands with 0 or no-data values prior to use.

Typical input: `cleaned EnMap_Hyperspectral data [cEnMap_HSI]`

 

---

### Step 2 — Ensure All Required Masking Has Been Done

Typically includes masking for water, vegetation, cloud, cloud shadow, snow, ice, or topographic shadow.

Typical input: `[cEnMap_vwmsk_HSI]`

---

### Step 3 — Select the Compositional Mapping Tool

Under the Hyperspectral drop-down menu, select the compositional mapping tool. In the settings, select:

- Input dataset: `[cEnMap_vwmsk_HSI]`
- Base data name: e.g., `[CompMap_]`
- Mineral to be mapped: e.g., white mica

Results will be added to a `[CompMap – Outputs]` folder in the layer list.

---

### Step 4 — Examine Relative Abundance Results

Turn on the legend for each layer via the three-dot menu → **Toggle legend**. The default relative abundance is between ~0.2 (high, red) and ~0 (low, blue) using a `jet` color ramp.

**Key questions:**
- Does the distribution match what you know about mineral presence in the AOI?
- For white mica, do results correlate with the MS product `[AlOH_b6 index]`?
- Are the patterns and distribution consistent with the multispectral mapping?

Note that CompMap results include contributions from all white mica species (paragonite, muscovite, phengite, illite) and may also include other Al-OH species.

Adjust the min/max values for the histogram in the settings menu to better fit your data distribution.

---

### Step 5 — Examine Composition Results

For **white mica**, the primary compositions to differentiate are paragonite, muscovite, and phengite, defined by the wavelength position of the ~2200 nm absorption feature:

- **Paragonite**: ~2185–2195 nm
- **Muscovite**: ~2195–2210 nm
- **Phengite**: ~2210–2225 nm

The best way to validate is to spectrally verify the composition of a selection of pixels across the project area using the Spectral Query tool.

**Key questions:**
- Does the species identification match the predicted results?
- Are other minerals being mapped as white mica in lower relative abundance areas?
- Is there a positional relationship between paragonitic vs phengitic mica and mineralization (e.g., Au) or structural features?

---

### Hillshade and Variable Alpha
URL: https://earthdaily.github.io/documentation/mining/using-marigold/hillshade-and-variable-alpha/

# Hillshade and Variable Alpha Tools

## Marigold 2.8.0 introduces new hillshade and spatially variable alpha settings.

Hillshade visualizations can be a powerful tool to transform and interpret your data — not just for topography, but also for geophysical datasets and mineral processing maps.

**Jump to:** [Add a Raster Layer](#add-a-raster-layer) · [Generate a Hillshade](#generate-hillshade) · [Apply a Hillshade](#apply-hillshade) · [Spatially Variable Alpha](#spatially-varying-alpha) · [Additional Examples](#additional-examples)

### Add a Raster Layer

Click the `+` symbol next to Raster layers and select `Catalog layer`. Locate `Copernicus Digital Elevation Model (DEM) GLO-30` under the topography section, select it, and click `Add selected layers`.

The resulting view shows the elevation model with the default `gist_earth` colormap. Modify the appearance through the settings menu or click the magic wand button for an automatic 2% contrast stretch.

### Generate Hillshade

Expand `Raster management` in the processing toolbox and select `Generate Hillshade`. Select your input Product and the input band, then adjust the settings below.

#### Sun Angle

0–90°. Controls the height angle of the illumination source — 90° is directly overhead. Lower sun angles produce more shadows and may hide terrain features.

#### Sun Azimuth

0–360°. Controls the cardinal direction of the illumination source — 0° north, 90° east, 180° south, 270° west.

#### Z Factor

Vertical exaggeration — higher values produce more contrast and shadows between subtle features.

Once happy with the result, optionally rename your output layer and click `Create Hillshade`.

### Apply Hillshade

Enter the `settings` of any raster layer and scroll to `Advanced Settings`. Check the `Apply hillshade` box and select your generated hillshade product.

#### Blending Modes

Four pixel blending modes are available: **Multiply**, **Hard Light**, **Soft Light**, and **Linear Burn**. We recommend a trial and error approach. You will also find sliders for `Brightness` (−1 to +1) and `Gamma` (default 1).

### Spatially Varying Alpha

Within Advanced Settings, control the alpha (transparency) of the layer based on data values from a raster layer. This can be applied to the entire layer, or only to the applied hillshade layer.

### Additional Examples

#### Alteration Map of Goldfield, Nevada

A hillshade from the Copernicus DEM applied to the Alteration mineral index over Goldfield, Nevada adds important geological context — some strong alteration regions form resistive ridges, while others are more recessive.

#### Magnetic Structures in Kalgoorlie Gold District

A magnetic hillshade applied to the RGB True Color Composite of Sentinel-2 BEC over Kalgoorlie, Western Australia, juxtaposing complex magnetic features superimposed onto satellite imagery.

#### Airborne Magnetic and Radiometric Surveys — Republic, Washington

Using new airborne surveys from the USGS [EarthMRI initiative](https://www.usgs.gov/earth-mapping-resources-initiative-earth-mri). Topographic, magnetic, and radiometric hillshades are combined to outline magnetic highs associated with local Cretaceous plutons.

---

### Product Update Utility
URL: https://earthdaily.github.io/documentation/mining/using-marigold/product-utility-tool/

# Using the new Update Product Utility

## How to update a Marigold `.sav` file when access issues occur due to subscription changes.

When transitioning subscription levels in Marigold, users may face access challenges with layers due to unique Product IDs used for Bare Earth Composites in the EarthDaily Catalog. Before working with `.sav` files post-update, users must update the Product IDs of affected layers using the new `Update Computed Layer` tool.

> *NOTE: Tiles in Marigold will return this error when a user does not have access to the products required to create them.*

### Using the Tool

1. Open the file in Marigold
2. Navigate to the `Processing toolbox`
3. Click on the `Raster management` dropdown
4. Click on `Update computed layer`

Select all layers to create a comprehensive list of affected Product IDs. It is recommended to select all layers.

Choose the new Product ID to replace the old one. If a product does not require conversion, simply leave it blank.

Choose to either **Overwrite** (recommended) or **Append** the layers:

- **Overwrite**: The chosen layers will be recreated with updated product IDs, retaining their original names. The project is automatically resaved as `MarigoldProject_updated.sav`.
- **Append**: The selected layers will be duplicated with `_updated` appended to their names.

Click **Update Layers** and the utility will convert the layers and automatically save the file.

Your original `.sav` file will remain intact, allowing you to revert if needed.

Questions? Email [support@earthdaily.com](mailto:support@earthdaily.com).

---

### Spectral Query Tool
URL: https://earthdaily.github.io/documentation/mining/using-marigold/spectral-query-tool/

# The Spectral Query Tool

## Marigold 2.6.0 brings a totally revamped spectral query tool.

The spectral query tool forms the backbone of advanced spectral analysis in Marigold, serving as the primary point of pixel interrogation as you learn the properties of your area of interest. The 2.6.0 overhaul provides more precise control over point selection, query naming, band ranges, and source products.

### Using the New Spectral Query Tool

Select `Spectral Query` from the dropdown next to the `Spectra` section of the left-hand panel.

> **Note:** The spectra menu has been simplified to group features that either (1) add spectra to the project, or (2) export spectra from the project.

#### Selecting Products and Bands

The tool opens as a panel on the right-hand side. Select a spectral product and modify the band selection — for example, toggle only the VNIR bands from the Fused Bare Earth Composite, or select a range of bands from 2000–2500 nm from an EnMAP scene.

Click `Update band selection` to view an overlay of those bands on the spectrum plot below.

With the new tool, you can take repeated spectra measurements while the tool is open without permanently adding them to the project. Users can rename and change the color of each spectrum before saving.

#### Querying the Scene

Click `Start querying` to begin. Click points on the map to obtain the spectrum for that pixel. Continue clicking until you right-click the map to end the session.

Collect as many spectra as you like and compare them live on the spectral plot. You can even change the product and compare spectra from multiple sources at once.

#### Rename and Customize Your Selections

Once happy with your samples, rename and modify the line color of each spectrum and discard any you don't need. The checkbox toggle next to each spectrum name determines which samples will be saved. Click `Add selected spectra` to close the dialogue and add your spectra to the left-hand list.

---

### Vector Upload Guidelines
URL: https://earthdaily.github.io/documentation/mining/using-marigold/vector-upload-guidelines/

# Vector Upload Guidelines

## With the 2.6.0 update, Marigold now supports more vector upload formats and coordinate systems than ever.

### Supported Formats

Previous versions of Marigold exclusively supported vector uploads in `.geojson` format registered in WGS84 (`EPSG:4326`). With the new changes, vectors in most common formats and projections can now be uploaded directly without reformatting or reprojection.

> **Remember:** Vector formats that consist of multiple files, like ESRI Shapefiles and MapInfo Tab files, must be compressed into a `.zip` folder before uploading.

#### `.geojson`

- Fully compatible as a single `.geojson` file.
- Still requires exclusively `EPSG:4326` due to GeoJSON convention. Uploading in other coordinate systems may result in vectors appearing in the incorrect location.

#### `.shp`

- Must be uploaded in a `.zip` archive including all associated files (`.shx`, `.dbf`, `.prj`, `.cpg`, etc.).
- Most coordinate systems supported.

#### `.tab`

- MapInfo Tab files must be uploaded in a `.zip` archive including all associated files (`.dat`, `.id`, `.map`).
- Most coordinate systems supported.

#### `.gpkg`

- Highly flexible; can contain numerous spatial and non-spatial tables.
- Current support opens and displays the **first spatial table** in the `.gpkg` file. Separate complex files into individual tables prior to uploading.
- Most coordinate systems supported.

#### `.parquet`

- A relatively new and highly efficient vector table format.
- Exports from EarthDaily's Iris software for ground deformation monitoring are provided in `.parquet` format and can be uploaded directly.
- Most coordinate systems supported.

#### `.dxf`

- AutoCAD DXF files — a common output from 3D modeling software like Seequent's Leapfrog.
- Marigold is limited to 2D geographical coordinates; 3D DXF files may not behave as expected.
- Due to the nature of the DXF format, no CRS is provided. DXF files are only supported in `EPSG:4326`. Uploading in other coordinate systems may result in vectors appearing in the incorrect location.

---

### 2.12.0
URL: https://earthdaily.github.io/documentation/mining/features-and-updates/marigold-2.12.0-new-features/

# Marigold 2.12.0 — New Features

## The first major release of 2026 — compositional mapping expansion, raster calculator improvements, and a reinvented autosave.

### Compositional Mapping 2.0

In 2025 we released the first iteration of our advanced mineral and compositional mapping tool with White Mica capabilities. In this update, we expand the `Compositional Mapping` tool to include additional minerals key to hydrothermal mineral systems:

- **Chlorite**: abundance, MgO composition, FeO composition, and MgO/FeO ratio
- **Alunite**: abundance and composition
- **Kaolinite**: abundance
- **Carbonate**: abundance

The tool assesses the shape of the hull-normalized spectrum for each pixel and matches the presence or absence of key spectral absorption features to determine mineral presence. The **absorption depth slider** controls the threshold for matching a mineral based on the depth of the key absorption feature. Mineral composition is defined by the characteristics of that absorption feature — specifically the wavelength position of the minimum.

The workflow has been redesigned to be simpler: switch between minerals using the tabs at the bottom, modify the absorption depth minimum slider to adjust the threshold, and all outputs are added to a dedicated folder.

> The hyperspectral mineral abundance and composition mapping tool is powerful, but always use the spectral query tool to assess the effectiveness of mineral maps and refine your results.

---

### Mineral Indices Revamped

#### Raster Calculator: Store Your Favorite Formulas

The `Raster Calculator` now allows users to **save and name favorite expressions** for reuse across different sessions. Saved expressions can be loaded directly from the Raster Calculator interface and overwritten if needed. To delete saved expressions, find the full list in the `User Settings` panel, accessible from the Gear icon in the top ribbon.

> Remember: band names and wavelengths may be product-specific — a formula built using PRISMA wavelength positions won't work for EnMap imagery because the band positions differ.

#### Rapid Mapping Outputs Update

The Rapid Mapping Outputs tool is the top spot for EarthDaily's curated list of mineral indices, RGB band visualizations, and TRatio combinations specifically selected for mineral exploration. In this update:

- **Non-mineral indices** section added
- **Hyperspectral datasets** are now supported in addition to multispectral
- This tool will ultimately replace the original Mineral Indices and Hyperspectral Mineral Index Analogs tools

##### Non-mineral indices

New non-mineral indices added to help with masking residual features in hyperspectral imagery:

- NDVI — Vegetation Index
- NDWI — Water Index
- MNDWI — Modified Water
- NDSI — Snow Index
- NDGI — Glacier Index
- BSI — Bare Soil Index

##### Hyperspectral Analogs

The capabilities of the `Hyperspectral Mineral Analogs` tool have been moved into the Rapid Mapping Outputs tool. The tool finds the closest available hyperspectral band within 50 nm to match the required input band. If no band is within 50 nm, the index will not be available.

> Hyperspectral analogs should be interpreted with caution — they substitute a single narrow band for a much broader multispectral band and may not capture the full spectral response.

---

### Autosave Reinvented

The latest version of Marigold includes a **major update to the Autosave feature**:

- Any project saved with a name now has its own dedicated autosave version
- Autosaving triggers quietly every time a layer is created, in addition to the 10-minute checkpoints
- From the Load Project menu, any project saved with the new update shows an autosave checkpoint if available
- The name of the current project is displayed at the top of your Marigold session

> Note: Autosaving does not overwrite your main project file. Use the **Save** button to lock in changes, or **Save As** to create a divergent copy.

---

### 2.10.0
URL: https://earthdaily.github.io/documentation/mining/features-and-updates/marigold-2.10.0-new-features/

# Marigold 2.10.0 — New Features

## Hyperspectral capabilities take a huge leap forward with the initial release of the Compositional Mapping tool, alongside KMZ/KML upload, PCA improvements, and more.

### Compositional Mapping Tool

The new Compositional Mapping tool allows geologists to rapidly map the occurrence and composition of key minerals to build alteration models that advance exploration targets. In this first release, mapping capabilities are provided for three minerals associated with hydrothermal alteration:

- **White mica** — abundance and composition
- **Kaolinite** — abundance
- **Chlorite (MgOH)** — abundance

For a full walkthrough, see the [Hyperspectral Compositional Mapping Tool guide](../using-marigold/compositional-mapping-tool-reko-diq.md) and the [Marigold documentation](https://mining-energy-docs.appsci-production.earthone.earthdaily.com/#marigold/using-marigold/processes/comp-map-basic.html).

#### Mineral Abundance and Composition Theory

The tool works by analyzing each spectrum in the scene and looking for the presence or absence of absorption features that qualify or disqualify the pixel for a specific mineral. For example, to identify white mica, the tool looks for an absorption feature around 2200 nm and 2350 nm, while checking for the absence of a feature at 2160 nm (which would indicate kaolinite instead). Once identified as white mica, the composition is measured by mapping the wavelength position of the ~2200 nm absorption feature between paragonitic (~2180 nm), muscovitic (~2200 nm), and phengitic (~2219 nm).

#### Using the Tool

Load hyperspectral imagery from the Marigold Catalog — EnMap, PRISMA, EMIT, AVIRIS, or proprietary imagery. Open the `Compositional Mapping` tool under the `Hyperspectral` header in the `Processing Toolbox`.

> **Tip:** Outputs will be created in a folder system placed below any un-foldered layers. To visualize results above your imagery, add your source data to a folder before running the tool.

Select your source product, click your desired mineral, and results will be generated automatically. A sliding parameter filters the minimum absorption depth to tune the output. A higher threshold maps fewer pixels.

---

### Additional Updates

- **KML / KMZ upload support** — Complex KMLs with mixtures of points, lines, and polygons will be separated into individual vector layers.
- **Vectorize classified layer** — The tool now has more intuitive parameter choices to control minimum polygon size.
- **Principal Components Analysis (PCA)** — The dialog will now automatically generate results without needing to apply them. Additional statistics including eigenvectors, eigenvalues, and percent explained variance are now available.
- **Spectra export additions** — Spectra can now be exported as ENVI formatted `.txt` files. Latitude-longitude coordinates for any spectra can also be downloaded via the three-dot menu → "Download geometry".

---

### 2.9.0
URL: https://earthdaily.github.io/documentation/mining/features-and-updates/marigold-2.9.0-new-features/

# Marigold 2.9.0 — New Features

## Rapid Mapping Outputs, improved Canny edge detection, Valley Bottom Flatness, UMAP, vector inspection tools, and a reorganized Processing Toolbox.

This release also coincides with the release of a [completely overhauled documentation page](https://mining-energy-docs.appsci-production.aws.descarteslabs.com/) with comprehensive guides to every tool and feature in Marigold.

### Rapid Mapping Outputs

Speed up your output products by automating the creation of mineral indices, RGB mappings, and TRatios using the new **Rapid Mapping Outputs** dialog, located under the Band Algebra section. This new tool allows you to use EarthDaily's predefined visualizations to rapidly generate mapping products from the Bare Earth Composite datasets.

The tool allows users to generate multiple outputs at once and provides the option to modify the contrast stretch and systematically rename the results. Select a BEC composite layer and choose up to three products for each calculation. RGBs typically look best using a 2–98% contrast stretch, while mineral indices may require more precise tweaking.

For more on the specific mineral index, RGB, and TRatio products available, visit the [updated documentation page](https://mining-energy-docs.appsci-production.aws.descarteslabs.com/#marigold/using-marigold/processes/mineral-indices.html) (subscribers only, password required).

---

### Spectral Library Changes

Marigold now has an updated dialog for adding spectra into your project with more flexibility, including:

- Searchable spectral libraries (currently case-sensitive)
- Option to add all selected spectra individually, or add their average
- Ability to **create your own spectral library** to collect and compile scene-collected spectra across Marigold projects

To create your own library, click the three-dot menu next to the Spectra section and select "Save spectra to spectral library". Provide a description and modify the project name if necessary.

---

### Canny Edge Detection

We have revamped the existing Canny edge detection tool to provide faster, cleaner outputs on the fly. Improvements include:

- Live updates while modifying parameters with a transparent background
- Reworked algorithm for handling edges and missing data around masked areas
- Reorganized — now found under the **Terrain Analysis** heading of the Processing Toolbox

For more on the input parameters and usage, see the [updated documentation page](https://mining-energy-docs.appsci-production.aws.descarteslabs.com/#marigold/using-marigold/processes/canny.html).

---

### Multiresolution Valley Bottom Flatness

Multiresolution Valley Bottom (and Ridgetop) Flatness (MRVBF and MRRTF) are algorithms that use DEMs to assess the flatness and lowness of terrain, identifying areas of valley bottom flatness that likely correlate to the depth of surficial deposits. Useful for geochemical sampling campaign design and hydrologic/geomorphologic applications.

Found in the **Terrain Analysis** section of the Processing Toolbox under **Valley Bottom Flatness**. The only input required is a choice of DEM — Copernicus, SRTM, or a proprietary DEM. Results are compiled into a unique Catalog product per DEM. The MRVBF product will have two bands: valley bottom flatness and ridge top flatness.

> Note: Only users with Compute Access will be able to use the MRVBF feature. Contact your organization administrator or EDA support with questions.

---

### UMAP

Uniform Manifold Approximation and Projection (UMAP) is a dimensionality reduction tool, similar to PCA or MNF, that can be applied to hyperspectral imagery to help extract spectral characteristics and identify patterns and similarities between units.

> Note: Only users with Compute Access will be able to use the UMAP feature. Contact your organization administrator or EDA support with questions.

---

### Vector Tools

**Vector inspection:** Click on a polygon or point vector object to view its column properties in a pop-up. To disable the inspector, click the three-dot menu next to your vector layer and select "Toggle popups".

**Calculate area:** Click the three-dot menu next to any polygon vector layer and select "Compute area". The total area in m² and km² will appear. Note: this returns the total area of all polygons within the layer.

---

### 2.8.0
URL: https://earthdaily.github.io/documentation/mining/features-and-updates/marigold-2.8.0-new-features/

# Marigold 2.8.0 — New Features

## Hillshade, splash page, hyperspectral mineral index analogs, and vector points and polylines.

### What's new?

- **Hillshade** — create shaded relief maps from any raster product and blend the results with your data. Tweak the final appearance with new variable alpha setting controls.
- **A new splash page** to help you jump back into your more recent projects.
- **Quick hyperspectral visualizations** — create multispectral analog mineral indices and ternary visualizations using approximate bands from hyperspectral datasets.
- **Vector points and polylines** — Marigold now supports drawing point and polyline features in addition to polygons.

---

### Hillshade and Variable Alpha

Visualize your data in Marigold like never before, with powerful hillshade capabilities to highlight topography, emphasize geophysics, and build beautiful maps.

For a complete tutorial, see the dedicated article: [Hillshade and Variable Alpha Tool](../using-marigold/hillshade-and-variable-alpha.md)

The new tool works in two steps. First, generate a hillshade layer from an input dataset like a DEM by modifying sun position and vertical exaggeration. Next, apply and blend that hillshade with any other raster layer through the new **Advanced Settings** dialog accessible from any layer's settings menu.

---

### Splash Page

When you first open Marigold, you will see a new splash page to help you dive in faster.

Options available from the splash page:

1. **Start a new project** — Jump in from scratch, optionally selecting a saved Bookmark location.
2. **Open a recent project** — A dropdown of your five most recent projects, each with a central coordinate reference on the mini-map.
3. **Open the Load dialog** — View all save files and sort by name or last-saved date.
4. **Upload a `.sav`** — Quickly load a `.sav` file sent by a colleague.
5. **Load the latest autosave** — Immediately reopen the latest `autosave.sav` to continue work after a disconnection.

---

### Mineral Index Analogs for Hyperspectral Imagery

A new tool in the Hyperspectral Toolbox allows users to create mineral index outputs from hyperspectral data that are analogous to those available in the multispectral toolbox. The tool selects the bands closest in wavelength to the selected mineral index or RGB to quickly produce an analogous output.

> Remember: Output products will not be equivalent to multispectral products because the bands have not been resampled over the broader multispectral wavelengths. Use this tool only as a proxy.

---

### Vector Points and Polylines

Users can now create **point** and **polyline** features directly within Marigold in addition to polygons.

Navigate to the `+` icon next to `Vector layers` and select `Draw layer`. Choose the type of vector product (point, polyline, or polygon). Click the pencil icon next to the layer to make it editable, then click the draw vector tool on the left side of the map window to begin drawing.

### 2.7.0
URL: https://earthdaily.github.io/documentation/mining/features-and-updates/marigold-2.7.0-new-features/

# Marigold 2.7.0 — New Features

## Folders, Bare Earth Composite metadata query, and consolidated multispectral/hyperspectral tools.

### Folders

Marigold 2.7.0 introduces a folder system within the Raster layers menu to help organize workspaces, particularly when managing numerous layers.

**Adding folders to an existing project:**
Click the `+` button next to Raster layers and select `Add new folder`. Enter a folder name and select the layers you'd like to add, then click **Assign**.

**Organizing new layers:**
Click the three-dot menu next to a layer and select `Folder management` to assign the layer to an existing folder or create a new one.

Folders can be rearranged within the layer order, toggled on/off with the eye icon, and collapsed or expanded to minimize visual clutter.

---

### Bare Earth Composite (BEC) Metadata Query Tool

A new raster utility answers the common question of which original date each pixel in a BEC mosaic was captured. To use:

1. Navigate to `Raster management` in the Processing Toolbox and select **View BEC Metadata**
2. Choose the specific BEC to query
3. Click **Collect metadata**
4. Click on the map to place points — the corresponding Sentinel-2 and/or ASTER acquisition dates will be returned

Right-click, move the map, or click **Cancel** within the tool to stop querying.

This is especially helpful when there are large time gaps between S2 and ASTER acquisitions, such as in areas where a mine has been developed between the two images.

---

### Consolidated Multispectral and Hyperspectral Tools

The hyperspectral-specific versions of transform and classification tools — such as Principal Components Analysis and Spectral Angle Mapper — have been enhanced to replace the original multispectral versions. The same MNF tool can now be used to process both Fused BEC and EnMap data. Each tool features a streamlined band selection interface, and for tools like PCA, a detailed statistical breakdown of the analysis results is now included.

---

### Additional Changes

- The Vectorize Classified Layer tool now identifies classified layers better, including results from k-means analyses and the mineral mapping tool.
- Added option to generate screenshots over selected vectors in addition to the entire viewport.
- Fixed issue where GeoTIFF exports did not properly remove regions masked by vectors.
- Fixed display issue for vector layers added from the Vector Catalog.

### 2.5.0
URL: https://earthdaily.github.io/documentation/mining/features-and-updates/marigold-2.5.0-new-features/

# Marigold 2.5.0 — New Features

## New ways to share save files, zoom-to for spectral query points, and the Product Update Utility.

### Sharing Save Files

Users can now share `.sav` files with individual users by email, or with their entire organization. Saving and sharing options are available through the save menu dialog.

To load a shared save file, open the Load Project menu and filter to show projects shared with you. These files will be shown with a `(shared)` suffix after their name. Note that shared projects still belong to the original creator — any work you perform will create a divergent copy, so it is recommended that you save the file with a unique name.

---

A new feature in the three-dot menu of any spectrum with an associated latitude-longitude allows you to **zoom-to** a spectrum's location on the map — particularly useful for power-users with dozens of spectra in their workspaces.

---

A new tool in the `Raster Management` section of the `Processing Toolbox` allows users to convert the base products used in derived layers — most commonly when a client has upgraded or downgraded between a global or continental Marigold subscription.

For full instructions, see the dedicated article: [Using the new Update Product Utility](../using-marigold/product-utility-tool.md)

## Mining > Iris

### Introduction
URL: https://earthdaily.github.io/documentation/mining/iris/getting-started/iris-introduction/

# Introducing Iris

## An online interface for viewing and analyzing InSAR results over engineered infrastructure sites.

Descartes Labs is proud to announce the release of Iris, a new online interface for viewing and analyzing InSAR results over your engineered infrastructure sites.

### InSAR Analysis at Descartes Labs

InSAR (interferometric synthetic aperture radar) is a powerful remote sensing tool that uses active sensor data to monitor large critical assets like tailings storage facilities. Subtle deformation measurable by InSAR has historically been shown to precede catastrophic failure events that can lead to loss of life, environmental damage, supply-chain disruptions, and major financial impacts.

Descartes Labs provides high quality deformation results using SAR imagery for a variety of applications and industries through a fast and automated pipeline called **GDS (Global Deformation System)**, developed by a team of in-house InSAR scientists. This product is the result of peer-reviewed research and has proven useful and accurate for remote deformation monitoring surrounding mining, civil engineering, and critical infrastructure.

Using the GDS pipeline, data from public or private satellite sources like Sentinel-1 or TerraSAR-X is ingested, processed, and delivered within **18 hours of collection** to provide mm-scale deformation measurements showing subsidence and uplift over manmade structures and natural features.

### Iris

Due to the scale of the spatiotemporal data produced by InSAR analysis, distribution and visualization of these data can be a challenge. Iris is a dedicated tool for viewing GDS results as soon as they are available, enabling users to make insights faster to drive decision making on the ground.

Iris includes a full suite of visualization and analytical tools, including state-of-the-art **anomaly detection algorithms** that can alert users to areas showing movement trends outside of their expected behavior. Additionally, subscribed users will have access to **Quicklook**, a tool that can produce on-demand deformation analyses using Sentinel-1 data at slightly lower resolution anywhere in the world — a fast and powerful tool for assessing regional trends or determining if an area warrants closer attention.

### Getting Started

This series of Knowledge Base articles is designed to get you started using Iris:

1. [The Iris Interface](./the-iris-interface.md)
2. [Data Layers in Iris](./data-layers-in-iris.md)
3. [Anomaly Detection in Iris](./anomaly-detection.md)

---

### The Iris Interface
URL: https://earthdaily.github.io/documentation/mining/iris/getting-started/the-iris-interface/

# The Iris Interface

## A Guide to the Layout and Design of Iris

**Jump to:** [Data Analysis Panel](#data-and-analysis-panel) · [Adding Data](#deformation-layers) · [Processing Tools](#processing-toolbox) · [Vector Data](#vector-layers) · [Exporting](#export-layer) · [Navigation Bar](#navigation-bar) · [Map Window](#map-window) · [Deformation Plot](#deformation-plot-and-controls)

### Getting Started

Iris is a cloud-based software accessible through any web browser, including Google Chrome, Microsoft Edge, and Apple Safari. Navigate to: 

If prompted, enter your Descartes Labs login credentials. Contact [support@descarteslabs.com](mailto:support@descarteslabs.com) if you have any difficulties accessing Iris.

---

### Data and Analysis Panel

Within the left-hand panel you'll find a variety of tools and features designed to help you add, adjust, analyze, and export your data.

#### Deformation Layers

The Deformation Layers section serves as the main control for the data displayed in Iris.

To add data to the session, click the `+` symbol. You will be presented with a list of available sites for viewing, including some demonstration analyses.

Upon selection, a precise analysis window can be chosen, with the most recent one selected by default. Relevant metadata for the site will also be displayed. Once the analysis has been determined, click **Add Layer**.

By default, the map window shows **Line of Sight (LOS)** results as the default data layer — the movement of each point towards or away from the satellite in millimeters over the observation period. If the analysis includes both ascending and descending satellite passes, the default layer will be **Up(+)/Down(−)**, showing vertical movement. The data layer can be changed in the drop-down menu. Full details on each data layer are explained in [Data Layers in Iris](./data-layers-in-iris.md).

The remaining Deformation Layers settings allow adjustments to the visualization:
- **Min/max values** for the linear histogram stretch
- **Mask Threshold** to filter out points with movement below a specified value (e.g., entering 10 eliminates points with less than 10 mm of movement)
- **Time slider** to track the evolution of deformation over time by stepping back through the analysis

#### Processing Toolbox

The processing toolbox contains settings and tools designed to extract insights from your InSAR results, currently focused on anomaly detection. Visibility of certain tools may vary based on your Iris subscription level.

**Stack Analysis:** Only available with a Quicklook subscription. Allows users to view burst footprints from Sentinel-1 and calculate deformation results anywhere in the world, on demand.

**Alerts:** A series of checkboxes to calculate and display alerts from the most recent data collection, as well as display historical alert data. See the dedicated article: [Anomaly Detection in Iris](./anomaly-detection.md).

**Optical Imagery:** Users with access to Descartes Labs' Standard or Premium Data packages can display additional raster images here, including Airbus SPOT imagery, NAIP, or Sentinel-2. Proprietary imagery such as drone imagery or lidar data can also be visualized through this menu.

**Derived Layers:** Calculated raster datasets including digital elevation models (Copernicus DEM, NASA DEM, and SRTM), slope and aspect layers calculated from SRTM, and Descartes Labs' proprietary **Global Velocity Layer** showing annual deformation data over large areas.

#### Vector Layers

Vector layers can be used in multiple ways in Iris. Polylines and polygons can be added or drawn within the map window to calculate and visualize deformation over a transect or averaged within an area. Iris currently supports uploading of `.geojson` files in latitude-longitude coordinate system.

**Drawing Vectors**

To draw a vector layer, click the `+` icon next to Vector layers and select between Polygon, Polyline, or Point.

Click the pencil icon next to your newly created vector layer's name to make it editable, then click the draw vector icon that appears on the left side of the map window. Click the map to add nodes and continue clicking until you are ready to finish. To complete a polygon, click the first point again. To complete a polyline, click the last point again to stop drawing. Click the pencil icon again to exit edit mode.

> Note: The area and transect plotting tools will only work properly with either a single polygon or polyline within each respective layer.

**Inclusion and Exclusion Polygons**

Polygon vectors can also be used as inclusion or exclusion vectors that can change the area used in each GDS analysis. This feature will typically be done in coordination with Descartes Labs support.

#### Export Layer

To work with data from an analysis in external software, results can be downloaded directly from Iris. In the Export Layer section, click the **Save Icon** to view an export menu and select **Download Analysis**.

Data downloads are provided in **Parquet file format** — a relatively new, open-source data format that stores large vector databases much more efficiently than formats like `.shp`, `.tab`, or `.geojson`. All `.parquet` files are provided in WGS84 Latitude-Longitude (`EPSG:4326`) and can be read by most modern GIS software, including ArcGIS and QGIS.

> Note: There is currently a known issue with `.parquet` files in QGIS for Mac — a workaround is available, please reach out if you have any issues.

---

### Navigation Bar

The Navigation Bar has a number of features to help you control the map window, including Bookmarks, Basemaps, zoom, and geographic coordinates.

#### Bookmarks and Location

The Bookmarks dropdown allows you to save the location and zoom level of the map window so you can quickly jump back to it. Click **Create Bookmark** to save your current view.

To navigate to a specific location, enter the WGS84 latitude and longitude coordinates in the box on the right-hand side, separated by a comma. Coordinates can be copied directly from Google Maps by right-clicking the desired location.

#### Basemaps

A number of free open-source basemaps are available:
- Street view and satellite view from OpenStreetMaps
- Topographic map and shaded relief map
- Open source geologic maps provided by [Macrostrat](https://macrostrat.org/)
- Light (white) and dark (black) background options

---

### Map Window

The map window is your main way to visualize data. It displays points from your GDS analysis, anomaly detection results, and vector layers, along with a scale bar and legends for your GDS data layer and anomaly layers.

Navigation is similar to other mapping programs — left-click to pan and use the scroll wheel or `+`/`-` icons to zoom. You can also maximize the map window to full screen mode.

The **green deformation pointer icon** corresponds to the data displayed in the deformation time series window when Point measurement mode is selected. Drag the green icon to any point of interest and the deformation time series plot will update automatically.

---

### Deformation Plot and Controls

The deformation plot shows a graphical display of your GDS data — either as a time-series (Point or Area mode) or as a cross-section (Transect mode). Controls above the plot let you toggle between measurement modes, select vectors for areas and transects, lock the Y-axis, and display standard deviation error bars where applicable.

#### Time-Series Plot

In **Point** or **Area** measurement mode, the plot shows Time on the X-axis and the selected Data Layer (e.g., LOS) on the Y-axis. In Point mode, the plot corresponds to the green pointer icon on the map and updates live as you drag it. In Area mode, the plot shows the average deformation within the defined polygon vector.

The leftmost point always represents epoch 0 (always a value of 0). Moving the time slider in the Data and Analysis Panel does not affect data displayed on the plot in these modes.

#### Transect Plot

When switched to **Transect** mode with a suitable polyline vector selected, the deformation plot becomes a cross-section view. The X-axis shows distance in meters along the polyline, while the Y-axis shows corresponding deformation at each intersecting point. As you hover your mouse over the plot, a corresponding symbol appears on the polyline in the map window.

In cross-section mode, the deformation data corresponds to the epoch selected in the time slider. Moving through the time slider updates the plot to show how deformation has progressed through the analysis period.

> Tip: Check the **Lock Y-Axis** feature on the last epoch before stepping back through time to keep a consistent scale for comparison.

---

### Data Layers
URL: https://earthdaily.github.io/documentation/mining/iris/getting-started/data-layers-in-iris/

# Data Layers in Iris

## Get to know the different data layers available in a GDS analysis.

Results from InSAR measurements like the Global Deformation System (GDS) are most commonly viewed in displacement values — millimeters of change. In addition to that key total deformation value, a number of other data layers are provided with each analysis to help contextualize the data.

---

### Line of Sight versus East-West-Vertical

#### Line of Sight (LOS)

Line of Sight data uses data from only one traverse direction of the satellite — either ascending or descending, but not both. The measurement is the change in distance between the satellite and the point of measurement in millimeters. Because SAR satellites including Sentinel-1 travel in polar orbits, the total displacement reported in LOS data represents not just vertical (up/down) change, but also horizontal change in the east-west direction.

#### East-West-Vertical (EWZ) Data

When a site is covered by both ascending and descending passes of a satellite, the right-looking and left-looking LOS analyses can be collated and the true east-west and vertical components of deformation can be calculated through trigonometry. Because the satellites travel in a polar orbit, **north-south components of movement can never be derived.**

When viewing EWZ data in Iris, you can select between the East-West and Up/Down components for each data layer and its derivatives, including uncertainty, velocity, and acceleration. By convention, western movement is negative and eastern movement is positive.

---

### Spatial Filtering

Deformation time series results from InSAR are relative in two ways — time and space. For time, LOS data is referenced to the first date in the analysis (epoch 0, always a value of 0). For space, a reference system must be chosen. Descartes Labs handles spatial referencing in two ways and provides both options to clients with each analysis.

**LOS (Spatially Filtered)**

The default LOS data layer has had a spatial filtering algorithm applied to remove larger patterns in the data and highlight more local deformation signals. A long-wavelength trend is fitted to the data and then subtracted from the raw data for each epoch. In most small-to-moderate scale sites this trend is roughly 1 km; in larger areas such as cities or regional features, the long-wavelength trend can be 3–5 km.

*Left: unfiltered data. Center: the estimated long-wavelength background trend. Right: spatially filtered results with background trend removed.*

**LOS (Unfiltered)**

When LOS (Unfiltered) is selected, an orange point marker with an anchor symbol appears in the map window. This point becomes the spatial reference point — all values displayed are relative to the orange marker. Users can place the orange icon on a location with high confidence of stability (e.g., a building on flat ground), then move the green icon through the scene to see all measurements referenced to that stable position.

**LOS Uncertainty**

LOS Uncertainty is useful when investigating a deformation signal and determining whether it represents genuine movement or falls within the noise of the data. Descartes Labs' novel methodology for assessing uncertainty can be [read in further detail here](https://www.preprints.org/manuscript/202206.0097/v1).

For a detailed explanation of spatial filtering methodology, see [Spatial Filtering in Iris](../technical-methodology/spatial-filtering-in-iris.md).

---

### Velocity and Acceleration

Velocity and acceleration provide another way to visualize GDS results. These values are delivered as single values based on a trend curve fit to the **past 180 days of data** for each point. Because these are static data layers, the time-series deformation plot will be inactive when either is selected.

- **Velocity**: provided in mm/day
- **Acceleration**: provided in mm/day²

---

### Coherence

Coherence is a property of InSAR data that reflects the noise in the radar signal. Hard, solid materials like rock, bare soil, concrete, or buildings will have high coherence, while soft, wet, or moving objects like vegetation, water, wet ground, and earth-moving activities produce noisy signals and lower coherence.

Coherence is calculated as a value from 0 to 1, with 1 being highly coherent, high-confidence data.

Descartes Labs applies a coherence threshold to its GDS results to ensure only high-quality points are returned with each analysis. Typically this value is set at **0.6**, but may be individually modified during initial setup to ensure sufficient coverage over a site. If you notice gaps in data over your area of interest, it is likely because those points did not meet the coherence threshold.

Viewing the coherence layer over your site and observing how it changes over time can give insight into how events like seasonal vegetation change or rainfall can affect the quality of your InSAR signal throughout the analysis window.

---

### Anomaly Detection
URL: https://earthdaily.github.io/documentation/mining/iris/getting-started/anomaly-detection/

# Anomaly Detection in Iris

## Understand changes at your site with confidence.

Descartes Labs delivers anomaly detection algorithms for GDS results that help identify potentially concerning movement over a site so that appropriate actions can be taken on the ground.

### Overview

Results from GDS analyses can contain millions of datapoints, which can be overwhelming and make it hard to identify areas that may require more attention. Analyses of known failures that have occurred on mining infrastructure and natural features indicate that the signals in InSAR data that precede these events can be subtle and complex, and are commonly not necessarily associated with the absolute total deformation of those points.

For that reason, Descartes Labs has developed an anomaly detection system that looks for statistically significant changes in the behavior of each point and highlights these areas into anomalies in three categories. Iris also gives you the ability to visualize alerts from previous analyses to help understand how these areas have moved or changed over time.

To calculate and view anomalies, activate the checkboxes within the **Processing Toolbox** in Iris.

---

### Current Anomalies

#### Steady

Steady anomalies are based on the **linear trend** of each point over the past 120 days. Linear movement can indicate that an area is slumping continuously through time, which can damage infrastructure even without a catastrophic failure.

To be classified as a Steady anomaly alert, points must have:
- A linear slope **above** a threshold
- An acceleration rate **below** a threshold
- A standard deviation of the linear fit thresholded based on velocity (lower velocity points have stricter requirements)

#### Sudden

Sudden anomalies focus on **more abrupt changes** to a point's deformation history. The conditions to qualify as a Sudden anomaly relate to both acceleration and velocity within the past 120 days of monitoring.

To meet the requirements, the polynomial fit to the time series must have:
- An acceleration term **above** a threshold
- A statistically anomalous increase in velocity within the **last 4 collects** (48 days using Sentinel-1 data)

#### Complex

When both Steady and Sudden anomalies are flagged for a given point, the point is classified as having a **Complex anomaly**. These points may warrant additional observation as their behavior shows both continuous movement with a significant increase in velocity over the most recent collections.

---

### Historical Anomalies

Two additional features allow you to visualize historical anomalies over your site in reference to those calculated for the most recent collection period. Viewing historical anomalies can give better context as to the severity and persistence of an anomalous feature.

- Small isolated anomaly polygons that occur within a given analysis but are absent in the collections before or after are less concerning.
- If anomaly polygons associated with an anomalous feature are consistent and growing or shifting with subsequent analyses, it may be more cause to investigate.

Both historical methods overlay anomaly polygons from the preceding two-thirds of the analysis window (240 days in the case of a 1-year Sentinel-1 analysis).

#### Timeseries Mode

Polygons are unfilled with the outline color corresponding to the date of the anomaly, scaling from old (dark blue) to recent (yellow). This helps determine if historical anomalies still represent a current issue or if the movement has dissipated.

#### Persistence Mode

Anomaly polygons are given a faint red opacity. Overlapping polygons become increasingly saturated as opacities compound — single-occurrence anomalies appear pale while persistent anomalies appear darker. This helps determine the severity of an anomaly over time.

---

### Anomaly Polygons

Anomalies are calculated on a point-by-point basis for each analysis, giving every point a state of either alerting (steady, sudden, complex) or not. For visualization, these points are polygonised and smoothed to give the vector outline polygons available in Iris. Polygons also must meet minimum size thresholds, and internal holes are closed during the smoothing process. It is therefore possible to have non-anomalous points within an identified anomaly polygon where the majority of the contained points met the requirements to draw the shape.

---

### DEM-Error Corrected Points
URL: https://earthdaily.github.io/documentation/mining/iris/technical-methodology/dem-error-corrected-point-locations/

# DEM-Error Corrected Point Locations

## New in Iris 1.5.0 — improved location accuracy in areas where the digital elevation model differs significantly from actual ground elevation.

To map SAR imagery to geographic locations, a DEM is required. However, publicly available global DEMs such as the **Shuttle Radar Topography Mission (SRTM)** and **Copernicus GLO-30** were collected 10–25 years ago and have become outdated in areas where open-pit mining has created large holes in the ground or tailings walls have been built up significantly. When more recent or high-resolution DEMs are provided, these are used instead — however in some instances, publicly available data is all that is available.

### DEM Errors and InSAR

Errors in the DEM can be identified with InSAR because they present as a phase contribution that correlates with the component of orbit variations. This allows InSAR to effectively estimate DEM errors. While this known effect has always been computed and accounted for when estimating the deformation time series, our recent work allows us to **improve SAR imagery co-registration** based on the estimated DEM error.

### DEM-Error Corrected Point Locations in Iris

Our team has researched the effects that DEM error can have on the precise location of points. Iris now includes a novel **repositioned points capability** that allows users to plot their points in the location that has been corrected for DEM errors.

We believe this will significantly strengthen the ability to assess the stability of slopes and monitor your assets. In many cases — such as with legacy assets or areas without large topography changes — there will be little to no difference between the DEM-error corrected point locations and the initial point locations. However, in areas where active mining has changed topography, there may be larger differences.

### Example

In the example below:

- **Figure 1** shows optical satellite imagery of part of an open-pit mine and the surrounding area.
- **Figure 2** shows the typical method for displaying InSAR results using a legacy DEM on a regular grid.
- **Figure 3** shows the DEM-error corrected point locations.

On the left side of the images, outside of the pit, there is little to no correction. Within the pit itself, which is actively being mined, points are noticeably shifted. Notice how many of the shifts coincide with the locations of benches — these did not exist in the original DEM, resulting in a DEM error and hence a co-registration error.

Iris now allows users to **toggle between the original points** (derived from legacy DEM standard regular grid) and the **repositioned points**, allowing comparisons and highlighting areas most affected by DEM-error estimates.

*Figure 1. Optical satellite imagery over an active mining operation visualized in Iris.*

*Figure 2. The typical method for displaying InSAR results in Iris, using a legacy DEM on a regular grid.*

*Figure 3. The "Use repositioned points" function is selected in Iris to show DEM-error corrected point locations. The active pit area on the right shows points shifting between Figure 2 and 3 due to improved co-registration capability.*

> Note: The DEM error estimation relies on InSAR phase that can contain other sources of error, such as transient partial decorrelation. For this reason, successive InSAR analyses may not estimate the DEM error and resulting point relocation completely consistently.

---

### Historical Consistency
URL: https://earthdaily.github.io/documentation/mining/iris/technical-methodology/historical-consistency/

# Historical Consistency

## Understanding historical inconsistencies in Iris InSAR analyses.

### Overview

Deformation estimates derived from synthetic aperture radar (SAR) data can change with successive analyses of the SAR data. These inconsistencies are due to the nature of the algorithms used to estimate deformation and due to unexpected changes in surface properties — referred to as **"the history problem"**. Iris includes a means to view the size of these inconsistencies to help users interpret the deformation results.

---

### InSAR-Based Deformation and the History Problem

A deformation time series derived from SAR data has an important property: the deformation reported at *a specific point in space and time* depends on the input SAR data at *every point in space and time*. This dependence occurs in several places.

SAR data is noisy, and the first step in the Iris deformation pipeline is to remove the noise. Given noisy data at times A, B, and C, the algorithms ensure that the change from A to B combined with the change from B to C equals the change from A to C — the data is required to be **temporally consistent** after noise removal. Note that estimating noise at time B depends on input data at A, B, and C, not just B. Points are included in the SAR analysis if the estimated noise is small.

Once there is a temporally consistent set of data, the Iris pipeline estimates **spatially consistent** data by creating a spatial network connecting neighboring points. The data along each link are adjusted so that the deformation difference between two points is the same regardless of the path through the network. This can be thought of as spatially integrating the changes along different paths through the network to arrive at point values.

*Fig 1: Optical data overlaid with "good" SAR points in red, where neighbors are connected by links in blue.*

The nature of SAR data leaves an ambiguity in the difference in each link. Resolving these ambiguities consistently (known as **unwrapping**) is a global spatial operation.

At this point the Iris pipeline has temporally and spatially consistent data. The final step is to remove any systematic contributions, primarily **atmospheric effects** and **orbit path variation**. These contributions are inferred based on spatial and temporal trends — essentially curve fitting that depends on all available data.

Iris always operates on a time window of at least a year of data. With every new SAR collection, Iris shifts this time window forward in time to include the most recent collection. The year-long window increases Iris' ability to de-noise data and identify and remove systematic contributions.

*Fig 2: An example where four year-long analyses exhibited different estimated deformation during the first half of 2024. Causes of historical inconsistency can include proximity to noisy points, steep terrain, and changes in surface property.*

---

### Iris Features to Assess the History Problem

As of January 2025, Iris analyses include ancillary data showing the **spread of historical results**. For analyses that include these ancillary data, the layer drop-down will include **"Historical LOS"** (or similar for east-vertical analyses).

Selecting **"Plot STD"** will show time series plots like the one below.

*Fig 3: Time series plot for historical data.*

The key elements of this plot are:

1. **Blue line** — the mean of the historical deformation, taken over the ten most recent available analyses, including the most recent one.
2. **Blue error bars** — the standard deviation of the ten most recent analyses.
3. **Red line** — the deformation for the most recent analysis.
4. **Red error bars** — the uncertainty estimates from the Iris pipeline.

All historical analyses are normalized to track deformation since the first date in the most recent analysis — historical data will always have a mean of zero at the first displayed date.

Note that only the most recent analysis provides data for the most recent date, and only the most recent two analyses provide data for the second-most-recent date. Therefore, at the most recent date, the mean is computed over a single element (the most recent analysis), and the historical standard deviation at the most recent date is zero.

These data allow the user to see how much a result may be impacted by historical inconsistencies, indicated by either a sharp difference in the historical mean (blue curve) from the most recent analysis (red curve), or large error bars associated with the historical data.

---

### Spatial Filtering
URL: https://earthdaily.github.io/documentation/mining/iris/technical-methodology/spatial-filtering-in-iris/

# Spatial Filtering in Iris

## A guide to the processing steps applied to both filtered and unfiltered data layers in GDS results.

Deformation time series results derived from InSAR are relative in two ways: the results can only show how the surface changed in time and in space relative to other points. This means that results must be referenced to an **epoch (time)** — typically the first one, with deformation at that epoch set to zero — and also referenced **in space**.

### The Spatial Reference Problem

Often results are referenced to a point **P**, with all deformation results reported relative to the deformation at P. InSAR-derived motion can be thought of as similar to periodic survey results where all elevation data is reported relative to a particular benchmark.

Ideally, P would be:
- At a location known to be stationary (completely stable)
- Close to the area of interest
- Located at a point where the SAR signal has minimal phase noise

It is often hard to satisfy all these constraints, which can lead to artifacts. For example:
- If P is at a location that is actually sinking, the InSAR results will report everywhere far from P as uplifting.
- If P is far from the area of interest, atmospheric effects will degrade the quality of the measurement.
- If the SAR imagery has lots of phase noise at P, that noise will impact all reported deformation results.
- A successive analysis may not include point P due to loss of coherence, making comparisons difficult.

For more background on the reference point problem, see this [HyP3 InSAR product guide](https://hyp3-docs.asf.alaska.edu/guides/insar_product_guide/#reference-point).

---

### GDS Spatial Filtering

To address the reference point problem, GDS uses a **spatial filtering algorithm** to remove the long-wavelength deformation trend from the data and isolate areas of localized deformation. The deformation at any point is reported relative to the surrounding deformation. Removing a large spatial trend preserves the qualitative deformation results without requiring a fixed reference point.

The image below shows an example over an open-pit mine, where the large subsidence of the pit wall is captured after removing the long-range spatial trend — the subsidence at the pit wall is distinct from large-scale regional subsidence.

---

### LOS (Unfiltered) — Manual Reference

The signal from spatial filtering can be recreated in the **LOS (Unfiltered)** layer by moving the orange reference marker to one of the stable points away from the pit wall. In this layer, spatial filtering has not been applied — deformation is reported relative to the orange marker, and moving the green test point to the orange marker would report identically zero.

---

### When to Use Each Layer

Spatial filtering solves a number of problems, but it does not work perfectly in all scenarios. For example, it may remove some of the actual signal to be measured, or a very large signal may bias surrounding data.

For this reason, Iris provides both:

| Layer | Description |
|---|---|
| **LOS** | Spatially filtered — long-wavelength trend removed. Good for identifying localized deformation. |
| **LOS (Unfiltered)** | Motion at the green point relative to the orange reference marker. Good for assessing differential motion across sharp boundaries. |
| **Up(+)/Down(−) Unfiltered** | Vertical component, unfiltered. |
| **East(+)/West(−) (Unfiltered)** | East-West component, unfiltered. |

We recommend placing the reference point (orange) at a spot **near the area of interest but outside the mining complex**. This layer is also useful for comparing motion across sharp boundaries to understand differential movement between points.
